PAPER: Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2026) 33:17 https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-025-02829-9 BRIEF REPORT All together now: Random Forests analysis reveals the joint impact of multiple statistical regularities on eye‑movements during reading Inbal Kimchi1 · Noam Siegelman2 Received: 27 August 2024 / Accepted: 28 July 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract A large and growing number of recent studies has embraced a statistical learning view of reading, revealing that readers uti- lize an array of regularities that are available in writing systems as they process printed words and texts. However, previous studies have focused on the impact of one regularity (or an otherwise small number of cues). Therefore, we currently have a limited understanding of (1) whether different regularities each carry unique explanatory power, beyond other (collinear) cues; (2) how do regularities at different levels of the input contribute to reading behavior; and (3) whether regularities vary in their contributions across processing stages. To answer these questions, we employ Random Forests analyses on a large- scale, eye-movement, passage-reading database from English first- and second-language readers, evaluating the relative importance of a large number of regularities on multiple eye-movement dependent variables. First, our findings demonstrate that, each regularity uniquely contributes to the model’s performance. Second, we show that both text-level regularities (e.g., predictability) and word-level regularities (including print-speech and print-meaning regularities), contribute to continuous text reading. Third, we document varying contributions of some regularities over time, with later reading measures being more impacted by text-level regularities. These results support and extend statistical learning theories of reading, showing that readers are attuned to a range of regularities in their writing system, which jointly guide naturalistic reading behavior. JSON: Name: rf_joint_regularities_reading Title: Random Forests analysis of eye-movement data to quantify the joint contributions of multiple word- and text-level statistical regularities to stages of naturalistic reading Short Hypothesis: When jointly modeled with standard psycholinguistic covariates, each measured statistical regularity (word-level: O-P, P-O, O-S, P-S; text-level: surprisal, semantic predictability, informativeness) will explain unique variance in eye-movement measures during passage reading, with word-level regularities contributing more to early measures (first fixation, gaze) and text-level regularities contributing more to late measures (rereading, total fixation), and these relative contributions will differ between L1 and L2 readers. Related Work: Existing research on reading has either focused on isolated regularities (predictability, informativeness, or single word-level mappings) or on standard psycholinguistic predictors (frequency, length) using linear/mixed-effect regression; such approaches are limited by predictor collinearity, unstable coefficient estimates, and difficulty capturing nonlinear interactions. A smaller set of studies applied tree-based methods to eye-movement data to estimate variable importance, but they used limited predictor sets or focused on structural complexity rather than a broad suite of word- and text-level statistical regularities. Work on word recognition has documented roles for orthography-phonology and orthography-semantics mappings but rarely evaluated their unique contributions in continuous text reading. Limitations in prior work include (1) testing predictors in isolation, (2) reliance on parametric models that perform poorly with collinear predictors and interactions, (3) limited cross-linguistic or L1/L2 comparisons, and (4) ambiguous mapping between predictor importance and processing stage. Abstract: Problem: Reading is shaped by many co-occurring statistical regularities in writing systems, but it is unclear which regularities explain unique variance in naturalistic reading and how their contributions vary across processing stages and reader groups. Approach: Fit Random Forests models to large-scale eye-tracking passage-reading data, jointly modeling standard psycholinguistic covariates and a broad set of word-level (O-P, P-O, O-S, P-S) and text-level (surprisal, semantic predictability, informativeness) regularity measures. Use cross-validated performance and normalized variable-importance scores to quantify each regularity's unique predictive contribution and compare early (first fixation, gaze) versus late (rereading, total fixation) measures and L1 versus L2 readers. Contribution: A reproducible pipeline that (1) evaluates unique explanatory power of multiple, collinear statistical regularities, (2) maps their relative impact across processing stages, and (3) contrasts L1 and L2 patterns. Expected outcome: Empirical evidence about which regularities jointly drive eye-movement behavior and how their roles shift over time and by reader type, informing integrated models of reading. Experiments: Datasets: MECO-L2 release (public): use full L2 sample (N≈498) and L1 subset (N≈45) reading the same 12 passages; align predictors to interest-areas as in original MECO preprocessing. Preprocessing: exclude interest-areas with total fixation <80ms or >2000ms, first fixation >800ms or gaze >1000ms; remove datapoints with missing predictor values; log-transform frequency, bigram frequency, neighbor counts as in source. Predictors: 15 predictors (word frequency, bigram frequency, word length, number of morphemes, orthographic neighbors, phonological neighbors, concreteness, age-of-acquisition; O-P consistency, P-O consistency, O-S consistency, P-S consistency, XGLM surprisal, semantic predictability cosine, word informativeness). Dependent variables: first-run skipping (binary), first fixation duration (ms), gaze duration (ms), total fixation duration (ms), rereading duration (ms), rereading (binary). Models: primary model = Random Forests via conditional inference forest (cforest) with ntree=1000, mtry in {3,4,5}, set.seed for reproducibility; compute permutation-based variable importance per tree and average; normalize importances to percentage of total importance per DV. Cross-validation: stratified 10-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times (or 90/10 train/test split repeated 100 times) to obtain held-out prediction metrics. Baselines: (1) linear mixed-effects models (lmer/glmer) with same fixed effects and maximal random effects structure where feasible; (2) gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) with matched training; (3) single-predictor models for frequency and surprisal. Evaluation metrics: continuous DVs = Pearson correlation and RMSE between predicted and observed values on held-out folds; binary DVs = accuracy, AUC. Statistical tests: permutation test for importance > 0 (10,000 permutations); bootstrap (1000 resamples) for CI of importances. Ablations: (A) remove all word-level regularities and measure drop in predictive performance and change in remaining importances; (B) remove all text-level regularities; (C) remove psycholinguistic covariates; (D) compare models trained on L1 vs L2 samples. Additional analyses: report stability of importance across mtry values and across CV folds; compute pairwise predictor SHAP-like contributions for selected trees to inspect interactions. Reporting: report normalized importance matrices per DV and group, held-out metrics, permutation p-values, and ablation effect sizes. Risk Factors and Limitations: Variable-importance bias: Random Forests permutation or split-based importances can be biased by predictor scale, collinearity, or category cardinality, complicating interpretation. Causality: importance indicates predictive contribution not causal influence; conclusions about processing mechanisms remain correlational. Predictor selection: results depend on chosen operationalizations (e.g., XGLM surprisal vs cloze), so omitted regularities may change inferences. L1 sample size: small L1 subset reduces power and stability for group comparisons. Measurement noise: eye-tracker errors, preprocessing thresholds, and unmodeled participant strategies can inflate noise and affect importances. Class imbalance: binary outcomes (skipping, rereading) may be imbalanced, biasing classifiers. Cross-dataset generalization: findings from English MECO may not generalize to other languages or orthographies. Computational cost: repeated cross-validation, permutation tests, and tree ensembles require substantial compute and memory for full-scale bootstrapping. Multicollinearity residuals: although tree methods tolerate collinearity, strongly correlated predictors can still distribute importance ambiguously across correlated sets, limiting precise attribution.
